section.title: Food Sacrificed to Idols
section.sectionRationale: The Corinthians boasted that they knew idols were nothing, so eating food offered to them was harmless. Paul agrees with the theology, there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom all things exist, but he confronts the arrogance of a knowledge that wounds. Love, not mere knowledge, must govern the use of Christian freedom, for the weak brother whose conscience is defiled is one for whom Christ died. To wound him is to sin against Christ.
section.thesis: Knowledge that there is one God and one Lord Jesus Christ is true, but knowledge alone puffs up while love builds up; so Christian freedom must be ruled by love for the weak brother for whom Christ died, since to wound his conscience is to sin against Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: knowledge puffs up but love builds up; the one God and the one Lord over against idols that are nothing; and the weak brother for whom Christ died, whom love will not wound.

units.label: Knowledge and love
units.note: knowledge puffs up, love builds up

verses.text: Now about {{eidolothyton|food sacrificed to idols}}: We know that we all have {{gnosis|knowledge}}. Knowledge puffs up, but love {{oikodomeo|builds up}}.
The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know.
But the one who loves God is known by God.
So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one.
For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords),
yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.

units.label: The weak brother for whom Christ died

verses.text: But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their {{suneidesis|conscience}} is weak, it is defiled.
But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do.
Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a {{proskomma|stumbling block}} to the weak.
For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?
So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge.
By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.
Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.

eidolothyton.gloss: Food, especially meat, that has been sacrificed to an idol. Much of the meat in a Greek city passed through pagan temples before reaching the market or the banquet. The question was whether a Christian could eat it, and the answer turns not only on truth but on love.

gnosis.gloss: Knowledge, understanding. The Corinthians prized it, and their knowledge that idols are nothing was correct. But Paul warns that knowledge by itself inflates the ego; only love, joined to knowledge, actually builds up the church.

oikodomeo.gloss: To build up, to edify, literally to construct a house. Set against puffing up, this word pictures love as the true builder of the community. The test of any exercise of freedom is whether it constructs and strengthens others or merely swells oneself.

suneidesis.gloss: Conscience, the inner sense of right and wrong. A weak conscience is one not yet fully persuaded that idols are nothing, so eating such food feels like real participation in idolatry. To press such a person to act against conscience wounds and defiles them.

proskomma.gloss: A stumbling block, an obstacle that causes someone to trip and fall. Paul warns that a believer's freedom, though legitimate, can become the very thing that trips a weaker brother into sin against his conscience, and so must be surrendered out of love.

basic.context: In Corinth most meat had first been offered in pagan temples. Some Christians said, we know idols are nothing, so we can eat whatever we like. Paul agrees that there is only one God and one Lord, so an idol is nothing. But he warns that knowing this can make people proud and careless. A newer believer, not yet free of his old idol worship, might be led by their example to eat against his conscience and be wounded. Since Christ died for that brother, to wound him is to sin against Christ. Love, not just knowledge, must decide how we use our freedom.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul affirms the strong believers' theology but corrects their attitude. The issue is not merely who is right about idols, but whether love governs the use of that rightness. The passage teaches a principle far beyond meat: the strong must limit their liberty for the sake of the weak, because people matter more than the exercise of a freedom.
basic.originalLanguages: The subject is eidolothyton, food sacrificed to idols. The Corinthians boasted in gnosis, knowledge, but Paul says love, not knowledge, does the true oikodomeo, building up. The weak have a tender suneidesis, conscience, not yet sure idols are nothing. And the strong must not let their freedom become a proskomma, a stumbling block, that trips a brother into sin.
basic.typology: The great confession that there is one God the Father takes up Israel's Shema, hear O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one, and astonishingly places the one Lord Jesus Christ within it. The self-giving of the strong for the weak follows the pattern of Christ, who did not please Himself but died for the weak.
basic.christ: Christ is confessed as the one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist, sharing the identity of the one God. And Christ is the measure of love for the weak: the brother in danger is one for whom Christ died, so to wound him is to sin against Christ Himself. The cross both reveals God and rules our relationships.
basic.god: There is one God, the Father, the source and goal of all things. The so-called gods of the nations are nothing before Him. This one God is not served by proud knowledge that harms others but by love that builds up, for the one who loves God is known by God.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 6 gives the Shema that Paul reshapes around Christ. Romans 14 is Paul's parallel teaching on the weak and the strong. 1 Corinthians 10 returns to food and idols, warning against the table of demons. Philippians 2 shows Christ not pleasing Himself, the pattern of surrendered freedom.
basic.oneStory: The one God who called Israel to confess Him alone is now known as Father and as the one Lord Jesus Christ. In His name the idols are exposed as nothing, and His self-giving love becomes the rule for His people: the strong lay down their rights for the weak, because Christ laid down His life for them all.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with the formula 'Now about', the same way Paul takes up the matters the Corinthians had written to him, 7:1, 12:1, 16:1. Chapters 8 to 10 are one sustained answer on idol food, and chapter 9 is not a detour but the middle panel of a three part argument: a principle in chapter 8, Paul's own case in chapter 9, and a warning plus practical rulings in chapter 10. Chapter 8 itself moves in three steps. Verses 1 to 3 set knowledge against love. Verses 4 to 6 grant the strong party their theology in full. Verses 7 to 13 then show what that theology costs when it is used without care.

The argument is built on a quiet reversal. Paul quotes a Corinthian claim, 'We know that we all have knowledge,' and agrees with it, then cuts it down in a line. Knowledge swells a person; love raises a building. He also turns the vocabulary of the strong back on them. The man with the 'well informed' conscience eats in the idol's temple, and his example 'builds up' the weak man, but the verb is used with bitter irony, because what is built is the courage to violate his own conscience, verse 10. Words that should mean growth end up meaning ruin, and the chapter ends with the word 'destroyed' in verse 11.

The confession in verse 6 is the doctrinal centre, and the whole chapter bends around it. It is carefully balanced, 'one God, the Father' and 'one Lord, Jesus Christ,' each with two prepositional phrases. After it, the tone shifts from theology to people, and the closing line is personal, with Paul's own vow in verse 13.
context.historical:
Corinth was a Roman colony and a busy trading city, and its religious life was crowded. Temples, shrines and dining rooms attached to sanctuaries were part of ordinary civic life. Meat was not simply bought and eaten at home. Much of what reached the market had first been offered at a temple, and a good deal of social eating took place in dining halls tied to a god, at weddings, society dinners and civic festivals. Refusing an invitation could mean giving offence to employers, patrons and family.

That is the pressure behind the Corinthians' question. The strong, probably better educated and better placed, reasoned that an idol is nothing and so a meal in its precinct is only a meal. The weak, many of them recently converted out of that very world, could not separate the food from the memory of the worship. For them the sight of a believer reclining in an idol's temple was not neutral.

Paul's own Jewish upbringing sits behind his position. Israel had been told to hold no other gods before the LORD, Exodus 20:3, and the Jerusalem council had asked Gentile believers to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, Acts 15:29. Paul does not simply repeat that ruling here. He argues from the gospel and from love, and he leaves room to eat meat bought in the market, as chapter 10 will say. Later, the risen Lord rebukes the church at Pergamum for the same cluster of sins, Revelation 2:14, which shows how long this issue stayed live in the churches of the Roman East.
context.canonical:
Verse 4 draws on the long Old Testament argument against idols. The prophets mocked the craftsman who burns half a log for warmth and bows to the other half, Isaiah 44:9-20, and the psalms say that idols have mouths that cannot speak and that those who make them become like them, Psalm 115:4-8. Paul's 'an idol is nothing' belongs to that tradition, though he will qualify it in 10:19-20, where demons stand behind pagan sacrifice.

Verse 6 rewrites Israel's central confession. Deuteronomy 6:4 says the LORD our God, the LORD is One. Paul keeps the two titles, God and Lord, which stood together in the Shema, and splits them between the Father and Jesus Christ without suggesting two gods. Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3 say the same of the Son: all things created through Him and for Him. Romans 11:36 gives the same pattern of 'from', 'through' and 'to' for God alone, so Paul is stating what the Bible says of the one God, and giving it to the Father and the Son together.

The weak and the strong reappear in Romans 14 and 15, where the same ruling is given with the same reason, 'for whom Christ died,' Romans 14:15. The ruling on food linked to idols returns in 1 Corinthians 10:14-33. Paul's own readiness to give up a right appears in chapter 9, and at the end of the letter, love is named as the way that surpasses every gift, 1 Corinthians 13:1-3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the strong party at Corinth to hear that being right is not the same as being loving, and that the church cannot be run by whoever has the best argument. He had no wish to dissolve their theology. He grants it, twice, in verses 1 and 4, and he states it better than they had. What he wants changed is the use they make of it. A believer who has grasped that idols are nothing has learned something true. He has not yet learned the thing that matters more, which is how to live with a brother whose mind has not caught up.

Paul also wanted them to see what the 'weak' believer is. He is not an obstacle to be managed, or an inferior to be tolerated. He is a person for whom Christ died, verse 11, and to wound his conscience is to sin against Christ, verse 12. That sentence is the hinge of the chapter and carries the weight of the whole command.

Finally, Paul meant his closing vow to be heard as an example, and as an invitation. He does not order the strong to give up meat for ever. He states what he himself would do, and in chapter 9 he gives the reasons that make such a vow sensible rather than extreme.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The details here are first century: meat from temples, dining halls attached to shrines, a church sorting out how to live in a pagan city. The chapter does not command believers today to avoid a specific food. The question about meat has no exact equivalent for most readers, and it would be a mistake to treat verse 13 as a rule about vegetarianism.

What the chapter prescribes is a pattern of reasoning that carries forward wherever Christians disagree over matters the Bible does not settle. Hold your convictions with gratitude, state the truth plainly, and ask what your freedom does to the person watching. Nor does the chapter tell the weak to stay weak. Paul expects growth, and the aim is that conscience be better informed, not that the most nervous person should rule the church. His concern is the manner in which a freedom is used, and especially whether someone is led to act against what he believes to be right, which Paul counts as sin even when the act itself is harmless, a principle he states in Romans 14:23.

debates.question: Who are the weak, and what exactly are they afraid of?

views.label: Gentile converts with a past in idol worship
views.case: Verse 7 says some are 'still so accustomed to idols' that they eat as though the food were sacrificed to an idol. This fits a convert from paganism, for whom the meal carried its old meaning. It is the most common reading, and it matches the picture of a city where nearly everyone had once been involved in temple worship.

views.label: Anyone whose conscience cannot yet follow the argument
views.case: Others note that Paul gives no ethnic label at all, and that the weak need not be one group. The category is moral and psychological: a believer whose conscience is not yet convinced, whatever its source. Romans 14 handles a similar situation among Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome, and the principle is the same.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree on the main point. The weak are not defined by their ignorance but by the fact that they would act against their own conscience if they followed the strong, and Paul counts that as real harm.

debates.question: Does verse 10 permit eating in an idol's temple, or only describe the strong party's practice?

views.label: It describes their practice, which Paul will forbid
views.case: Paul reports what the strong do, 'eating in an idol's temple,' and objects to its effect on others. In 10:14-22 he then forbids sharing in the table of demons. On this reading chapter 8 argues from love first, and chapter 10 adds the harder ground, that such meals are themselves a form of idolatry.

views.label: Paul concedes the point for argument, then closes the door
views.case: Some think Paul first argues on the ground of love because the strong would not listen to an argument from idolatry. He lets their premise stand, shows that it still leads to harm, and in chapter 10 gives his fuller answer, that a meal at an idol's table is a form of fellowship with demons. Chapter 8 is then the opening move and chapter 10 the full reply.

debates.bearing: The text leaves Paul's reasoning visible. He argues first from love and only later from the nature of idolatry, so that the strong who accept the first cannot escape the second.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's first word for the topic, eidolothyton, is a compound of 'idol' and 'sacrificed,' and it names the very thing the council at Jerusalem asked Gentile believers to avoid, Acts 15:29. It appears in Revelation 2:14 and 2:20 in the rebuke of Pergamum and Thyatira. In 1 Corinthians it names the question, not the answer.

The verb in verse 1, 'puffs up,' is phusioo, to inflate. It is a favourite word in this letter, used of the arrogance Paul charges against some of the Corinthians in 4:6, 4:18, 4:19 and 5:2, and its opposite in 13:4, 'love is not puffed up.' Here it is set against oikodomeo, 'builds up,' the house building verb. The two verbs give the chapter its design: a person can swell like a bubble or be built like a house.

Verse 3 turns the sentence around. Paul does not write that the one who loves God knows God. He writes 'is known by God,' using the perfect passive of ginosko. The tense points to a relationship begun by God and still standing. Christians who boast in what they know have misplaced the direction of knowing.

In verse 9 the BSB says 'freedom,' but the Greek is exousia, the very word for 'right' that carries Paul's argument in chapter 9, where he calls his claim to support an exousia in 9:4 to 9:6, 9:12 and 9:18. The link is deliberate: the Corinthians' right to eat and Paul's right to be paid are the same kind of thing, a real authority that love may decline to use. The weak person's conscience is described as defiled, from molyno, the verb of staining a garment, used in Revelation 3:4 of clothing soiled, and so the picture is of something clean made dirty.

Verse 11 says the weak brother is 'destroyed,' from apollumi, the word for perishing, and the verb is in the present tense, so Paul speaks of a process underway and of a real danger, not merely of an unpleasant feeling. In verse 12 the strong are 'wounding' the conscience, using a verb of striking, as of a blow. Verse 13 closes with 'stumble,' skandalizo, from the noun skandalon, the trigger of a trap. Paul's vow is the strongest form of refusal in Greek, a double negative with an aorist subjunctive and 'for ever' added, which is why many translations render it 'I will never eat meat again.'

typology.type: The Shema reshaped, Deuteronomy 6:4 and 1 Corinthians 8:6
typology.fulfillment: Israel's daily confession named the LORD, the one God, and Paul splits the divine name and title between the Father and Jesus Christ. This is not a new theology bolted onto the old one. It is the same one God, now known in the Son through whom all things were made and by whom believers live. The correspondence lies in the vocabulary, since both statements speak of oneness and of God and Lord. The escalation is that Jesus is placed inside the confession, not beside it. The type falls short only in being a spoken creed, because the fullest confession is a life that is lived through Him.

typology.type: Meat offered in temples and the sacrifices of the law
typology.fulfillment: Under the law, food and sacrifice were bound up with what was clean and unclean, and priests lived by what was offered, Numbers 18:8-24. Idol temples imitated and distorted that pattern. Paul's answer is that no food is able to bring a person closer to God, verse 8. What the law's food rules pointed toward is realised in Christ, who makes the person clean rather than the meal, Mark 7:18-19 and Romans 14:14. The type falls short because it was a set of rules about meat, while its fulfilment concerns the heart, and a clear conscience before God.

typology.type: The strong carrying the weak, Romans 15:1-3
typology.fulfillment: The picture of the strong bearing the weak is patterned on Christ, who as Paul says 'did not please Himself,' Romans 15:3. In chapter 8 the pattern is a command. In Christ it is a history: the one who was rich became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and the one in the form of God took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. The escalation is that Christ bore the weak at the cost of His life and not merely of a meal. The correspondence falls short because the strong at Corinth lay aside a freedom, while Christ laid aside glory and then died.

study.christ:
Chapter 8 leads to Christ in three ways. The first is by identity. Verse 6 places Jesus Christ inside the Shema. 'One Lord' is the title Israel gave to the LORD in Deuteronomy 6:4, and Paul says the same Jesus through whom all things came is the one through whom believers exist. Colossians 1:16 says the same, and so does John 1:3. Paul does not argue for this. He assumes it in a creed he expects the Corinthians to accept, and that tells us how early the church confessed the deity and the creating work of the Son.

The second is by value. The sentence that decides the chapter is 'this weak brother, for whom Christ died,' verse 11. Paul prices a person by the cross. The believer who seems to matter least in the congregation was worth the death of the Son of God. That is why wounding his conscience is a sin against Christ, verse 12, as though the injury were done to the Lord Himself. Jesus said as much, that what is done to the least of His brothers is done to Him, Matthew 25:40.

The third is by pattern. Paul's vow in verse 13 does not stand alone, and it is not heroics. It follows the one who 'did not please Himself,' Romans 15:3, who being rich became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and who emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. The strong at Corinth were being asked to do on a small scale what Christ did on the largest scale. In the same way Jesus warned against causing little ones to stumble, Matthew 18:6, and spoke of the cost.

The passage also guards against a misuse of Christ. Knowledge of Christ that leaves a person proud has not understood Him, because the one who is truth is also the one who stooped. The measure of knowing Christ is what it does to our dealings with His other people. A caution is needed here as well: the chapter does not teach that weaker believers set the rules for the church, or that Christ requires everyone to give up every liberty. It teaches that those who know the cross should handle a brother's conscience as Christ handled them.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter says about God is that He is one, and that this oneness is a relief and not just a doctrine. Because there is one God, the many 'so-called gods and lords' of verse 5 have no claim on anyone. Paul does not deny that people worship such things, and in 10:20 he will say that demons are active behind them. His point here is that none of them is God, and none can alter the nature of a piece of meat. That frees a believer from fear of food, of festivals and of the old powers.

Second, He is the source and the goal. 'From whom all things came and for whom we exist' is a statement about our purpose. We were made by Him and for Him. Romans 11:36 says the same. The Christian life is therefore not a negotiation of what is allowed. It is the life of creatures who have been given back their place, and who can ask in every circumstance what the God who made them would want.

Third, He is a God who knows His people before they know Him. Verse 3 does not say the one who loves God is known by God as a reward for loving. It says the love is the sign that God's knowing has already taken hold. For people who were worried about what they knew, this is a comfort. The weak, whose knowledge is thin, are as fully known as the strong whose knowledge is wide. God does not rank His people by what they can explain.

Fourth, He cares for the weak with a particular tenderness. He has given them a conscience, and He treats its violation as serious. The same God who owns the whole earth, so that no food is unclean in itself, Psalm 24:1, will not let His children treat a brother's tender conscience as a small thing.

In worship, this means that confessing 'one God' includes a way of treating one another. A church that sings of the one God and then runs over its weakest member has not yet heard its own confession. The chapter invites a worship that is humble in knowledge, generous in love, and clear that the Father and the Son are together the object of praise.

crossReferences.note: The Shema, Israel's daily confession that the LORD our God, the LORD is One. Paul's 'one God, the Father' and 'one Lord, Jesus Christ' keeps both of the Shema's titles and shares them between the Father and the Son, which is why many readers find here an early statement of the deity of Christ.

The same ruling given to the church at Rome. The same phrase, 'for whom Christ died,' appears in verse 15, and the same ruling follows: a believer may not let his freedom become a stumbling block. It shows that the teaching in 1 Corinthians 8 was Paul's settled pastoral pattern.

The strong ought to bear with the weak and not please themselves, because Christ did not please Himself. This gives the model behind Paul's vow in 1 Corinthians 8:13: the reason for self restraint is the pattern of the Son, not a list of rules.

Paul returns to the same matter and widens it. Everything is permissible but not everything builds up, and he adds practical cases about meat from the market and meals at an unbeliever's house, ending with the call to do all things for the glory of God.
Knowledge without love is empty. Chapter 13 states at length what chapter 8 states briefly, that love is the more excellent way and that even great knowledge, without it, amounts to nothing.

The Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to abstain from food sacrificed to idols. Paul's treatment in Corinth shows how that ruling was applied: with attention to conscience, to the nature of idolatry and to love for others.

The classic mockery of idols: made by human hands, with mouths that cannot speak, and those who make them become like them. It stands behind Paul's confident 'an idol is nothing at all in the world,' though he later adds that pagan sacrifices involve demons.

Jesus warns against causing one of His little ones who believe in Him to stumble, in the strongest terms. Paul's concern for the weak conscience reflects the same teaching, that harm to a vulnerable believer is a serious matter to the Lord.

Humility, looking to the interests of others, and the self emptying of Christ. This is the fullest New Testament statement of what Paul asks the Corinthian strong to imitate, and it shows that the cross is the pattern for the use of liberty.

The risen Christ rebukes Pergamum because some held to Balaam's teaching and ate food sacrificed to idols. It shows the question was not a Corinthian oddity, and that the churches of the Roman world faced real moral danger when meals joined them to pagan worship.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with one Creator and one human family, and the rest of the story is the damage done when people give to something made the honour owed to the Maker. Romans 1:25 describes that exchange. The idols of Corinth are one chapter in that long history, and the law and the prophets spend centuries calling Israel back from them. Paul's confession in verse 6 is the story in miniature: everything comes from one God and is meant to return to Him.

What this chapter adds is the arrival of the Son in the middle of that confession. The one God of Israel is known as the Father, and the Lord through whom all things came is Jesus Christ. That is the story's turning point, because the God who made the world has entered it for the sake of those who were lost in it. The weak brother for whom Christ died is the clearest proof of how far the Creator will go.

The chapter also shows what redeemed people are for. In Eden the first man and woman were given freedom and one boundary, and they used the freedom to serve themselves. Here, redeemed people are given freedom and are asked to spend it on others, as the new humanity under the last Adam. The strong lay down their rights in imitation of the One who laid down His glory, and in that small act the shape of the new creation shows up in a church.

The story ends with every false god gone. Revelation looks to a day when the nations bring their glory into a city where nothing unclean enters, Revelation 21:24-27, and the one God and the Lamb are its light. Then there will be no more food that tempts, no weak conscience to wound and no idol to fear. Until then, the church lives in the interval, confessing one God and one Lord, and showing in how it treats its weakest members that the confession is true.

quiz.q: What does Paul say is the difference between knowledge and love?

options.text: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
options.note: Verse 1 contrasts knowledge that inflates with love that edifies.

options.text: Knowledge is worthless and love is all that matters.
options.note: Paul affirms the truth they know; he insists love must accompany it, not replace it.

options.text: Love puffs up and knowledge builds up.
options.note: This reverses Paul's words.

options.text: Both knowledge and love always build up equally.
options.note: Only love is said to build up; knowledge alone can inflate.

quiz.q: What does Paul confess about God and Christ in verse 6?

options.text: There is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist.
options.note: Verse 6 places Jesus within the identity of the one God of Israel.

options.text: There are many gods and many lords for Christians.
options.note: Paul says the so-called gods are nothing; for us there is one God and one Lord.

options.text: Jesus is one lord among several equal powers.
options.note: Paul confesses Jesus as the one Lord through whom all things came.

options.text: The Father alone is God and Christ is merely a creature.
options.note: Paul joins the one Lord Jesus to the one God, sharing the work of creation.

quiz.q: Why should the strong believer limit his freedom to eat?

options.text: So his freedom does not become a stumbling block that wounds the weak.
options.note: Verse 9 warns that freedom can trip a weaker brother into sin.

options.text: Because eating such food is always sinful.
options.note: Paul says food itself does not bring us closer or further from God.

options.text: Because knowledge does not matter at all.
options.note: Knowledge matters, but it must be governed by love for the weak.

options.text: Because the strong believer will lose his salvation by eating.
options.note: The danger is to the weak brother's conscience, not the strong one's salvation.

quiz.q: How serious is it to wound a weak brother's conscience?

options.text: It is a sin against Christ, for the brother is one for whom Christ died.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 say wounding the weak brother is sinning against Christ.

options.text: It is a minor matter of personal preference.
options.note: Paul treats it with utmost seriousness as sin against Christ.

options.text: It concerns only the weak brother, not Christ.
options.note: Paul says it is ultimately sin against Christ Himself.

options.text: It matters only if the brother actually falls away.
options.note: The wounding of the conscience itself is already sin against Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul say he would do rather than cause a brother to stumble?

options.text: He would never eat meat again, surrendering his freedom out of love.
options.note: Verse 13 shows Paul willing to give up a real right for a brother's sake.

options.text: He would insist on his rights regardless of the weak.
options.note: Paul does the opposite, laying down his freedom.

options.text: He would demand the weak brother grow stronger first.
options.note: Paul places the burden on the strong to yield, not on the weak to catch up.

options.text: He would eat privately but not publicly.
options.note: His vow is more sweeping: never eat meat if it trips his brother.

questions: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Where might you be more concerned with being right than with building others up?
Paul confesses one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. How does placing Jesus at the center of your view of God shape your worship and daily life?
A weak brother's conscience can be wounded by another's freedom. Whose conscience should you be more careful of, and how might your example be affecting them?
Paul was willing to give up meat entirely for a brother's sake. What genuine freedom might love call you to lay down for someone weaker in the faith?
To wound a brother for whom Christ died is to sin against Christ. How does remembering that Christ died for the person in front of you change the way you treat them?

translationNotes.note: Food sacrificed to idols renders a single term for meat that had passed through pagan sacrifice; the phrase names the practical question behind chapters 8 to 10.
One God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, reshapes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4, including Jesus within the identity of the one God, a foundational statement of Christian faith.
For whom Christ died grounds the appeal: the weak brother is not expendable but one Christ valued enough to die for, so wounding him is sin against Christ.
